passage:
The clock on the tower at Orlen Cross stopped at ten past four one Tuesday in March. My grandfather, Aurel Moss, had kept it for forty-one years, climbing the worn iron ladder each Sunday to wind it, and that spring I had begun to climb with him. That weekend he had been at his sister's, and before he left he handed me the key. On Monday the Harl bus had left by the clock to the minute.

We went up together after breakfast. Pigeons had built their nests on the outer ledge, birds settling in for the spring, a skin of ice still clung to the face, and the hands moved freely when he tried them. Every pin and part of the escapement was sound, and the weight cable sat on its drum among the gears. He took out his notebook, where every winding since 1983 had a line and a date, and turned to the last page. The line for Sunday was blank. I had spent that day at a friend's house, with the key in my coat.

At the council meeting that evening, Jonas Brede from the hardware shop brought a catalogue of new electric works to replace the old, at a cost that would need a vote. Petra Vell, who chaired the council, spoke first about the Harl bus. Its driver set off by the tower clock, and that morning he had left forty minutes late with half the school aboard. She asked how soon the clock could be trusted again. My grandfather said by morning, and someone asked about his safety on the ladder.

Petra struck a bargain with me before the meeting closed. I would wind the clock every Sunday until the end of term, at two pounds a week, and my grandfather would check my work. I wound it that night, and it started at once.

The spring fair opened three weeks later with the bell ringing noon. I wound the clock each Sunday, and Petra paid me what she had agreed. In June the key went back to my grandfather. I spent the summer stacking paint tins at Jonas Brede's shop.

passage:
Lune's starwort, a pale blue flower about the size of a thumbnail, grows only on the north slope of Corrow Ridge. For a decade its seed heads have come up nearly empty, a serious matter for a plant that lives only four or five years. What brought Ines Varga, an ecologist at Pellham University, up the ridge in 2023 was a 1988 photograph she came across in an old field guide, in which the slope is blue from the treeline to the crest.

Everyone at Corrow had an explanation. Petra Moss, the park's warden, blamed the late frosts, and so did Aldo Brisk, who has grazed his sheep on the slope for more than thirty years. Varga decided to test every idea at once. Her student, Tobin Hale, staked out twenty-five plots where the starwort still grew thickest. Some were fenced against the sheep, some sheltered under cloths on frosty nights, some watered in dry weeks to keep the soil moist through the summer, and some cleared of crowding grass. On the last set Hale did the bees' work himself with a paintbrush, dabbing pollen from flower to flower.

In September Ruth Callan, who teaches at the village school in Ottery, brought her pupils up to count seeds. One set of plots stood out: the flowers Hale had brushed held about forty seeds a head, against four or five everywhere else on the slope. The starwort, it turned out, was simply short of bees.

The board met a week later, and it was Moss who proposed the motion. She had blamed the frost for ten years, and she set that aside without a moment's fuss. The vote was unanimous, and the plan is simple: Hale will spend next July on the slope with his paintbrush, doing again what he did this year.

The grant will cover the cost of keeping him there, and it was found in a single meeting, on the strength of one summer's counting, by a board willing to hear that its own warden had been mistaken. Public bodies seldom move so quickly, or change course so gracefully. This July, for the first time in a decade, the starwort will have help in time.
